tier_reason: The repo page and README carry only a qualitative claim; the comparison numbers against xz, Brotli, Zstd, Lz4 and Snappy live in the peer-reviewed ICDE 2025 paper (DOI 10.1109/ICDE65448.2025.00122 cited in the README), which is blocked here and was seen only through WebSearch snippets, and the repo harness (main_simd.cpp, benchmark/neats_lossless.cpp) has its baseline calls commented out. C stays a placeholder: B is warranted once the paper's tables are read, and A only if the paper states optimization flags (snippet gives Xeon Gold 6140M and GCC 13.2.1).

corrections.claimed_speedup: README text, no numbers on the page: NeaTS provides, simultaneously, compression ratios close to or better than the best existing compressors, a faster decompression speed, and orders of magnitude more efficient random access. Paper (ICDE 2025, arXiv 2412.16266) numbers seen only in WebSearch snippets, not on an opened page: compression ratios close to Xz/Brotli with up to 1 order of magnitude faster decompression and 3 orders of magnitude faster random access; compression ratio better than Lz4 by 52.77% and Snappy by 50.20% on average, and better than Zstd on almost all datasets by 28.49% on average.
corrections.hardware: Paper setup per a WebSearch snippet of arXiv 2412.16266v1 (not opened): Intel Xeon Gold 6140M, 1.17 TiB RAM, CentOS 7. The repo states no hardware.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Paper (WebSearch snippet only): C++23 compiled with GCC 13.2.1; optimization flags not seen. Repo CMakeLists.txt sets C++23 and CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS -march=native -mtune=native -mfpmath=sse -mavx512f -fno-math-errno; -O9 and -funroll-loops appear only in CMAKE_C_FLAGS; no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE default is set, so a plain 'cmake ..' build of the C++ code has no optimization level.
corrections.caveats: Paper numbers could not be read: arXiv, IEEE and the author's talk slides are blocked here, and no PDF or result table is checked into the repo (root has LeaTS.cpp, NeaTSL.cpp, SNeaTS.cpp, main_simd.cpp, CMakeLists.txt; benchmark/ holds Chimp, Chimp128, Gorilla, TSXor sources, neats_lossless.cpp, gp_compressors_bench.hpp, st_compressors_bench.hpp; the datasets are on a d4science link not opened). What the search snippets said, not verified on any opened page: NeaTS reaches compression ratios close to xz and Brotli with up to 1 order of magnitude faster decompression and 3 orders of magnitude faster random access (talk-slide snippet); fastest decompression on 10 of 16 datasets; ratio better than Zstd by 28.49% on average, better than Lz4 by 52.77% and Snappy by 50.20%; faster compression than LeCo by 36.26% and ratio better by 12.80% on average; compared compressors Xz, Brotli, Zstd, Lz4, Snappy, Chimp, Chimp128, TSXor, DAC, Gorilla, LeCo, ALP. A snippet figure of 2561.31 MB/s decompression for NeaTS next to PLA 2997.00 and AA 2420.20 appears to belong to the lossy NeaTS-L comparison against PLA and AA, so it is not used as the lossless claim. Repo evidence is thin: benchmark/neats_lossless.cpp main() currently runs only squash_scan with lz4 and has everything else commented out; main_simd.cpp prints NeaTS compression, random-access and full decompression speed but its final 'Decompression speed' line times a SIMD copy of the raw data, not NeaTS; LeCo and ALP are not in the repo harness; no CPU model or build flags are given. The README's plain 'cmake ..' sets no optimization level for C++ code (only the C flags have -O9), so a default build is unoptimized unless -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release is passed. Tier C is a placeholder: the paper is peer reviewed (B), and A is possible if it states CPU, compiler and flags since the comparator harness is public; retier when arXiv 2412.16266 or the IEEE page is readable. Files opened: raw README.md, CMakeLists.txt, main_simd.cpp and benchmark/neats_lossless.cpp of and-gue/NeaTS; github.com/and-gue/NeaTS, /commits, /tree/main/benchmark, /tree/main/lib, /tree/main/include. Verifier additions (2026-10-03): a WebSearch snippet of the arXiv HTML (2412.16266v1, not opened) gives the paper's setup as an Intel Xeon Gold 6140M with 1.17 TiB RAM, CentOS 7, C++23 code compiled with GCC 13.2.1; no optimization flags appeared in the snippet, so A still cannot be granted from what was seen. The CSV line of main_simd.cpp does time NeaTS simd_decompress (50 runs, with a value-initialized output vector allocated inside the timed loop) and random access (1e6 random indexes, 10 runs, integer ns per query), so the harness for NeaTS itself is real; the baseline side lives in squash_full/squash_random_access calls in benchmark/neats_lossless.cpp that are commented out except one lz4 scan. Co-author Giorgio Vinciguerra keeps a copy at github.com/gvinciguerra/NeaTS (not marked as a fork, shares the history up to 2025-07-15) with 10 more commits through 2026-03-08, including 'Use double precision if compression with float coefficients fails', 'Fix allocated size not multiple of alignment' and 'Remove architecture-specific compilation flags'; the first suggests the float-coefficient configuration (the default T1=float32 in main_simd.cpp) could fail on some inputs, and that copy's CMakeLists.txt still sets no C++ optimization level. The README says the code is 'released for academic purposes under the terms of the GNU General Public License v3.0'; the license itself is plain GPL-3.0, which allows any use.

notes: Record is accurate about the repo: README has no numbers, neats_lossless.cpp main() runs only squash_scan('lz4'), main_simd.cpp's last 'Decompression speed' line times a raw SIMD copy, and CMake sets no C++ -O level. Metadata confirmed on github.com (GPL-3.0, 13 stars, last commit 2025-07-15, so stale); the co-author's copy gvinciguerra/NeaTS is active through 2026-03-08 and may be the better link later. Retier to B once arXiv 2412.16266 or the IEEE page is readable.

tier_reason: README tables compare tsl::htrie_map with std::unordered_map and cedar::da; the benchmark code is public (gist Tessil/72e11891fc155f5b2eb53de22cbc4053, bench.cpp and Makefile with g++ -std=c++11 -march=native -DNDEBUG -O3) and the README states GCC 6.3, Debian Stretch and an Intel i5-5200u. An independent public harness (kampersanda/dictionary_bench, g++ 7.3.0, Release -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native, Xeon E5-2680 v2) reproduces the roughly 3x memory win over std::unordered_map.

corrections.caveats: The speed win holds against other tries (cedar::da, the C hat-trie, qp trie, crit-bit, Judy), not against hash tables: on the Wikipedia set std::unordered_map was faster (590.88 vs 643.10 ns insert, 173.58 vs 250.87 ns read), and the Askitis win over std::unordered_map is small (1.14x insert, 1.35x read) and reverses on insert if std::unordered_map is given reserve (309.06 vs 485.45 ns insert, while read stays behind at 109.89 vs 77.80 ns). The memory win over hash tables is partly caused by std::string keys costing at least 32 bytes each in those baselines (the README says so). Numbers are from 2017 hardware (laptop i5-5200u) and GCC 6.3. The gist (bench.cpp, Makefile) was read through WebFetch only, because gist.githubusercontent.com is blocked here, so flags and timing code come from the fetch tool's extraction; the README says best of 20 runs while the gist timing code looked like a single pass per invocation. Independent run, same insert and lookup protocol, found in the poplar-trie README (opened) on a Xeon E5-2680 v2 2.80 GHz, g++ 7.3.0 -O3, code at kampersanda/dictionary_bench (CMakeLists.txt opened: Release default -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native): Wikipedia titles Sep 2018, 14,130,439 keys: tsl::htrie_map 0.43 GiB, insert 0.60 us/key, lookup 0.27 us/key; std::unordered_map 1.29 GiB, 0.50, 0.27; cedar::da reduced trie 1.19 GiB, 0.89, 0.59. UK-domain URLs, 39,459,925 keys: htrie_map 2.68 GiB, 1.08, 0.51; std::unordered_map 6.05 GiB, 0.67, 0.50; cedar::da prefix trie 2.02 GiB, 2.20, 2.28 (the cedar prefix trie uses less memory than htrie_map on this set, 2.02 vs 2.68 GiB, but its lookup is about 4.5x slower, 2.28 vs 0.51 us/key). That run confirms about 3x less memory than std::unordered_map and no speed win over it. Files opened: README.md of Tessil/hat-trie (raw), gist 72e11891fc155f5b2eb53de22cbc4053 (WebFetch), github.com/Tessil/hat-trie and /commits, raw README.md of kampersanda/poplar-trie, raw CMakeLists.txt of kampersanda/dictionary_bench, github.com/kampersanda/dictionary_bench. Verifier additions (2026-10-03): the 3.1x memory figure against cedar::da uses the plain double-array trie; cedar::da's double-array prefix trie is much closer, 496.54 MiB on unsorted Wikipedia (about 1.23x htrie_map's 402.25 MiB) and 712.59 MiB on the Askitis set (about 1.18x of 601.79 MiB), and in the poplar-trie run it is 0.63 GiB against 0.43 GiB on Wikipedia (ratios derived from page data). In the README's sorted Wikipedia run (keys inserted and read in alphabetical order) htrie_map beats std::unordered_map, 255.76 vs 594.85 ns insert and 68.08 vs 173.54 ns read (about 2.3x and 2.5x, derived from page data), but sorted access is a favorable locality case and there cedar::da ORDERED=false prefix trie inserts faster (187.98 ns) and cedar::da double-array trie reads faster (54.72 ns). The hash-table baselines, std::unordered_map included, use CityHash64 rather than std::hash, so the std::unordered_map rows are not the out-of-the-box configuration. The category fit is loose: a HAT-trie is a memory-efficient dynamic trie, not a succinct structure.

notes: Every number in claimed_speedup matches the README rows and the derived ratios check out (3.12x/3.10x memory, 1.71x insert and 2.22x read vs cedar::da; 3.51x/1.83x memory, 1.14x insert, 1.35x read on Askitis). The win is memory, not speed against hash tables; metadata confirmed (MIT, 876 stars, last commit 2025-11-11, active, not a fork).
